Vandalur Zoo Diary

Field notes · VIT Chennai

An Industrial Visit to Vandalur Zoo

Two and a half months on campus, one bus ride out, and a day among peacocks, macaws, a very still crocodile and a tiger in a pond.

Stop 1 of 7

The Gate

Stepping past the gate of VIT Chennai after two and a half months of continuous campus confinement felt less like an educational excursion and more like being granted conditional parole. After months of surviving on scanners, strict hostel curfews and the endless saga of applying for leaves, the simple act of boarding a bus and crossing the campus perimeter was an emotional event. Half of us stared out the windows with bewildered eyes taking in the sights of local tea stalls and traffic as if we were explorers re-entering civilization after a prolonged expedition.

By the time the bus pulled up to Vandalur Zoo and we walked into that stretch of natural greenery and thick bamboo forest the collective sigh of relief was almost louder than the bus engine.

Stop 2 of 7

First Meeting

A peacock on the paved walkway.

Our first close meeting happened on the paved walkway, where a peacock wandered freely. The bird had royal-blue feathers on its neck and chest with a brown-and-white pattern on its back. One of my classmates quietly tried to walk beside it matching its steps. The peacock just stopped, gave him a quick look and waddled off into the bushes.

Stop 3 of 7

The Aviaries

Macaw, sun conure, Egyptian vulture and emus.

Further along the path we spent time at the aviaries watching different kinds of birds in large wire enclosures. A close look at the blue-and-yellow macaw showed its bright yellow chest, blue wing feathers, a dark patch under its beak and thin black lines across its white face.

Nearby a sun conure sat calmly on a green bamboo tube behind a grid mesh. It had a mix of yellow and orange on its head and body with green and blue on its wings.

In another enclosure an Egyptian vulture rested on a wooden branch. It had a white body, a spiky crown of feathers and a bare yellow face with a sharp hooked beak. It bore an uncanny resemblance to anyone who rolled out of bed five minutes before a morning lecture and sprinted across campus without combing their hair.

Across from the birds tall emus walked with long steady steps. Their shaggy brown-and-black feathers covered their bodies as they moved along their area.

Stop 4 of 7

The Primates

A lion-tailed macaque, a sign, a pile of bottles and a chimpanzee.

We then moved into the primate section. A lion-tailed macaque was sitting up in the trees. It later settled on a rock ledge against a painted forest background. With its jet-black coat and thick silvery-grey mane around its face it sat perfectly still—kind of like a student trying to stay awake during an early morning lecture.

The sign said one thing. The corner said another.

Nothing sums up the irony of our zoo visit better than standing in front of an official green sign declaring the area a strict plastic and litter-free zone—complete with threats of a Rs. 2,000 fine or imprisonment under the Wildlife Protection Act—only to walk around the corner and stumble upon a mountain of discarded plastic water bottles dumped right on the ground near the restrooms. It was a stark reminder of the massive gap between campus rules on paper and actual enforcement in reality, showing that while the zoo works hard to protect wildlife, managing human waste remains its toughest challenge.

In another enclosure a chimpanzee walked across an elevated orange concrete beam that was built over a water trench. Its strong body and dark fur stood out as it moved on all fours balancing easily on the ledge. Watching it walk across with complete composure felt like a quick lesson in poise—displaying a level of core stability and balance that engineering students can only pray for when trying to keep their grades afloat during midterms.

Stop 5 of 7

The Reptiles

A green iguana at the glass and a crocodile by the pool.

The reptile section had glass panels and natural setups for close viewing. A green iguana pressed against the glass showing its turquoise-green scales, a row of spiky spines down its back and large round scales along its jaw.

Near a sloped concrete pool a huge crocodile lay still on the dry ground. Its tough armored skin blended perfectly with the soil making it look like a stone statue. It was an example of saving energy—something we totally understood after a long week of assignments.

Stop 6 of 7

The Big Mammals

An Indian rhinoceros and a Bengal tiger.

In the mammal areas we saw an Indian rhinoceros near a central stone feeding trough surrounded by upright log posts. Its thick grey skin formed folds over its shoulders and back and its single horn was clearly visible as it sniffed around its food area.

At the end of our walk we reached the cat enclosure and saw a Bengal tiger partially in a shaded water pond behind a heavy wire fence. The tiger floated calmly its head and back above the green water. It was using a way to cool off—one we deeply envied while standing outside in the Chennai heat our water bottles getting warm.

Stop 7 of 7

Back on the Bus

After getting back on the campus bus that day it became apparent what the trip meant after all. While visiting Vandalur Zoo provided a welcome change from our regular classes and getting a chance to see animals in person it also turned out to be a perfect example of the best and worst parts of modern environment management. Seeing natural-like landscapes that were integrated into the urban setting helped us realize that such conservation work was needed in urban settings where natural areas faced a constant threat due to urbanization.

However, the stark contrast between the sign prohibiting plastic use and the nearby piles of plastic bottles by the toilets taught us lessons that would not have been possible if presented through slides during class. In this case it became evident that sustainability meant not imposing regulations but establishing proper waste management, reusing the resources, and changing the behavior of people. Being engineering students from VIT Chennai we returned home knowing that sustainable development was not a theoretical concept covered only in classes for exams but rather a problem that requires practical and well thought out solution.
